title: The Slave Who Invented Modern Vaccination
event_summary: During a devastating smallpox epidemic in Boston, an enslaved West African man named Onesimus told his owner Cotton Mather about a practice from his homeland: deliberately introducing material from a mild smallpox pustule into a small wound to produce immunity. Mather persuaded physician Zabdiel Boylston to test the method on 248 Bostonians, and only 2% of the inoculated died compared to 15% of the uninoculated population. This became the first statistically documented inoculation trial in the Western world, decades before Edward Jenner's more famous cowpox vaccine.
why_forgotten: Crediting an enslaved African man with foundational medical knowledge was ideologically inconvenient for a slaveholding society built on assumptions of Black intellectual inferiority. Mather himself was a complicated, often reviled figure after the Salem witch trials, and the violent backlash from Bostonians who threw a grenade through his window made the entire episode something the medical establishment preferred to distance itself from. Jenner's later work with cowpox became the cleaner, more palatable origin story for vaccination.
why_it_matters: Onesimus's testimony introduced the concept of deliberate immunization into Western medical practice, setting in motion the epidemiological reasoning that led to modern vaccination programs saving billions of lives. The Boston experiment also pioneered the use of comparative mortality statistics to evaluate a medical intervention, essentially inventing the concept of a controlled public health trial. Every modern vaccine mandate, every eradication campaign from smallpox to polio, traces its intellectual lineage back to knowledge an enslaved man carried across the Atlantic.
